notes:
I've put together notes for most of 2 Kings 6, but several parts of the brief came up empty. I found almost nothing for parts 2 and 3. I ran out of searches before reaching the Catholic, Orthodox, modern-scholarship, Lutheran, Methodist or prosperity sites, so those views are left out. Two pages also cut off partway: Precept Austin's after verse 1 and Enduring Word's partway through verse 29.

# 2 Kings 6: research notes

## Part 1: The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- **What "sons of the prophets" means:** Precept Austin says they were "not biological sons but describe a prophetic training community, like a spiritual seminary or ministry school." It adds that they were not monks: some were married (2 Kings 4:1). — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-6-commentary
- **A meeting hall, not a home:** Ellicott says the phrase really means "the place where we sit before you," a common hall for teaching. Whether it was the one at Gilgal or at Jericho is uncertain. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/ebc/2-kings-6.html
- **What the growth shows:** Guzik says the crowding shows that Elisha had a significant impact on the nation. The old building could no longer hold everyone who wanted training. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-6/
- **A contrast with Gehazi:** Precept Austin, quoting Hampton Keathley III, sets this faithful, hard-working group against greedy Gehazi in chapter 5. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-6-commentary

**v. 2**
- **Plenty of timber:** Ellicott notes that the Jordan valley was well wooded. If everyone helped cut trees, the work would soon be done. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/ebc/2-kings-6.html
- **A lesson on hard work:** The Pulpit Commentary says ministers and students for the ministry should be hard-working, as these students were. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-6.html

**v. 3**
- **Elisha's approval:** Guzik says Elisha did not start or lead the building project, but it could not happen without his approval and blessing. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-6/
- **Asking for the master's presence:** James Smith (quoted on Precept Austin) points out that only one man asked Elisha to come. He compares people who care about the building fund but not about Christ's presence with them. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-6-commentary

**v. 5**
- **Why the loss mattered:** Guzik says iron existed in Israel but it was not common enough to be cheap. The man was rightly upset because the tool belonged to someone else. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-6/
- **"Borrowed" may mean "begged":** Guzik quotes Wiseman, who says the Hebrew could mean the axe head had been asked or begged for, not necessarily borrowed. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-6/
- **A silent request:** The Pulpit Commentary says the man asks for nothing directly, but the tone of the complaint constitutes a sort of silent appeal. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/6.htm
- **Iron tools:** The Pulpit Commentary adds, citing Deuteronomy 19:5, that the Hebrews had iron axe heads as early as Moses' time. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/6-5.htm

**v. 6**
- **What "float" means:** Ellicott says the axe head did not swim, but simply rose to the surface. It had fallen in near the bank. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/ebc/2-kings-6.html
- **Why the stick:** For Ellicott, throwing the stick was a symbolic act. It showed onlookers the event was supernatural, and that God's power could make iron float like wood. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/ebc/2-kings-6.html
- **God uses means:** Guzik calls it a plain miracle with no trick involved. He quotes Spurgeon, who saw no link between stick and iron yet said "God does use means, and he would have us use means." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-6/
- **Small troubles matter to God:** Ellicott's moral is that God helps in small personal troubles as well as in great ones of larger scope. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/ebc/2-kings-6.html
- **A natural explanation, rejected:** Precept Austin mentions a theory that Elisha simply pushed the stick into the axe's handle-hole and lifted it out. It rejects this, because the writer clearly treats the event as one of Elisha's "wonders." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-6-commentary

**v. 7**
- **The man's part:** Guzik says God did what only He could do and left the man to do his part. He quotes Patterson and Austel: by picking it up, the student would personally participate in the miracle. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-6/

**v. 8**
- **Ambush tactics:** The Pulpit Commentary says the Syrian king planned a war of surprise ambushes, not open battle. It was cunning more than strength that the king relied on. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-6.html
- **Why war again so soon:** The Pulpit Commentary notes this follows closely on the Naaman episode. It explains that hostility was the normal state between the two countries, and a few years would dim the memory. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/6.htm

**v. 9**
- **Why help a corrupt king:** Guzik says Elisha did not back Israel's corrupt kings. But Syrian conquest would be worse, so he passed on intelligence God gave him. He quotes Dilday: the prophet was now the king's trusted adviser, not his enemy. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-6/

**v. 10**
- **More than once:** Ellicott says "not once nor twice" means Elisha warned the king on several occasions, about different Syrian raids. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-6.html

**v. 11–12**
- **"No traitor here":** The Pulpit Commentary reads the servant's answer as "there is no traitor in thy camp or in thy court." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/6-12.htm
- **God sees every secret:** The Pulpit Commentary says nothing escapes God's notice. It was Elisha's God who made the communication to him. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-6.html
- **Who the servant was:** Gill suggests he had heard of Elisha from Naaman, or had gone with Naaman to Israel. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/6-12.htm

**v. 13**
- **Dothan:** Clarke thinks it is the same place as the Dothan of Genesis 37:17. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-kings-6.html
- **The folly of the plan:** Whedon points out how blind it was to think a man who knew the king's secret plans could not also defeat his spies. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/6-13.html

**v. 15**
- **Who the servant was:** Ellicott says this is not Gehazi, who is never called Elisha's "minister" and is usually named. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-6.html

**v. 16**
- **Who "those with us" are:** Gill says Elisha meant the legions of angels that encamped around them. Barnes says Elisha voiced the conviction of all God's people when the world persecutes them. — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng//2-kings/6-16.html
- **A real reason, not wishful thinking:** Guzik says Elisha gave his servant an actual reason not to fear, even though the servant could not see it. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-6/

**v. 17**
- **Seeing what is already there:** Guzik says Elisha did not pray for anything to change, only for the servant to see what was real. Only God can open eyes to spiritual reality. He quotes G. Campbell Morgan: "Faith is never the imagining of unreal things." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-6/
- **The angels were real:** Clarke stresses that the fiery chariots were there, before the eyes of Elisha's servant were opened. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-kings-6.html
- **The servant's weaker faith:** Barnes says the servant lacked his master's faith. Elisha prayed he might see the angelic host as if with his bodily eyes. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/2-kings-6.html
- **Why chariots and horses:** Ellicott notes these were the strength of Aram's army. God shows that He too has chariots and horses, and they are made of fire. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/ebc/2-kings-6.html

**v. 18**
- **A text question:** Ellicott prefers the reading of the Syriac version and Josephus, in which Elisha and his servant went down *to* the Syrians. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/ebc/2-kings-6.html
- **What kind of blindness:** See the debate in Part 3.
- **Judicial blindness:** The Pulpit Commentary calls it a judicial act of God in response to Elisha's prayer. It draws a parallel with spiritual blindness. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-6.html
- **God gives sight or blindness:** Guzik says God may grant sight or send blindness as He sees fit, in answer to His people's prayers. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-6/

**v. 19** (the deception: see also Part 2)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Elisha meant the Syrians to understand that this was the wrong road and the wrong city. In the morality of the time, and, indeed, in the morality of all times up to the present, it has been held to be justifiable to deceive a public enemy. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/6.htm
- **Guzik:** Elisha told a technical truth but certainly intended to deceive. The lesson Guzik draws is that the spiritually blind are easily deceived. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-6/

**v. 20**
- **The shock of waking:** The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary describes their amazement at finding themselves inside Samaria, at the mercy of Jehoram's soldiers. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/6-13.html

**v. 21–22**
- **Prisoners of war:** Ellicott sums up Elisha's point: the men are as good as prisoners of war, so they must not be killed in cold blood. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-6.html
- **Pulpit Commentary's reading:** Elisha's question compares the king's case with Deuteronomy 20:13. Since the king did not capture these men himself, he could not justify killing them. Showing kindness might also soften the Syrian king toward peace. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/6.htm
- **Mass killing:** The Pulpit Commentary adds that even in the Old Testament there is probably no example of God approving the killing of a crowd who were not captives taken in lawful war. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-6.html
- **Romans 12:** Bible Hub links the passage with Romans 12:20–21, "if your enemy is hungry, feed him." — https://biblehub.com/2_kings/6.htm

**v. 23**
- **Obeying in spirit:** The Pulpit Commentary says Jehoram obeyed not just to the letter but in spirit, holding a grand banquet (citing Josephus). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/6-23.htm
- **The stress is on "raiders":** Ellicott says the Syrians stopped small, secret raids and instead tried all-out war (v. 24). Gill reads it the same way. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/ebc/2-kings-6.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/6-23.htm
- **Kindness won:** Guzik says answering evil with good changed the raiders' behaviour. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-6/

**v. 24**
- **Ben-hadad's name:** Ellicott suggests his full name may have been Ben-hadad-idri, "the son of Hadad is my help." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/ebc/2-kings-6.html
- **The king's heart unchanged:** Guzik says kindness changed the raiders but not their king, who launched a full siege meant to starve the city into surrender. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-6/

**v. 25**
- **The donkey's head:** The Pulpit Commentary notes the donkey was unclean (Leviticus 11:4) and its head the worst part. Keil and Delitzsch agree. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/6-25.htm
- **"Dove's dung":** The meaning is debated. See Part 3.
- **Judgment for apostasy:** Constable sees the siege and famine as the Lord's punishment for Israel's apostasy, citing Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/6-28.html

**v. 27**
- **The king's reply:** Ellicott says "If the Lord does not help you" is the right translation. He notes other possible renderings, such as "May the Lord not help you!" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/ebc/2-kings-6.html

**v. 28–29**
- **How bad it was:** Guzik says the cannibalism shows how terrible the famine was. He links it to the warnings of Deuteronomy 28. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-6/
- **The story itself:** GotQuestions describes how the second woman broke the agreement and hid her son. — https://www.gotquestions.org/dove-droppings-five-shekels-silver.html

**v. 30**
- **Why he tore his clothes:** The Pulpit Commentary says it was horror at what the woman's story revealed. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/6.htm
- **The sackcloth:** The Pulpit Commentary (Spanish edition) says we can hardly deny he felt some real repentance. But he was far from truly humble. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/spa/tpc/2-kings-6.html

**v. 31**
- **Why blame Elisha:** The Pulpit Commentary says this is unclear. Perhaps he thought Elisha could work any miracle whenever he liked. If so, he misunderstood the nature of the miraculous gift. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/6.htm
- **Beheading:** The Pulpit Commentary (Spanish edition) notes the Law never authorised beheading. The king was acting like other Eastern despots who treated their subjects' lives as their own. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/spa/tpc/2-kings-6.html

**v. 32**
- **"Son of a murderer":** The KJV's phrase points back to Ahab's murder of Naboth and the prophets, says Ellicott: the son takes after his father. Ellicott adds that Hebrew can call a man "son of" a trait he shows. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/ebc/2-kings-6.html
- **Elisha knew ahead:** Ellicott says Elisha knew in advance what was about to happen (compare 2 Kings 5:26). — https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-6.html

**v. 33**
- **Who is speaking:** Ellicott says the speaker is the king, and he accepts the correction "king" for "messenger" (*melek* for *mal'ak*). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/ebc/2-kings-6.html
- **What the king means:** Ellicott paraphrases him: why not surrender and kill the prophet who has fed me false hopes? — https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-6.html
- **Earlier talks about waiting:** The Pulpit Commentary infers that Elisha had earlier urged the king to "wait for" God. The king now says the time for waiting is over. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/6.htm
- **The king came after his messenger:** The Pulpit Commentary suggests Jehoram partly regretted his hasty order and hurried after the messenger. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/6.htm

## Part 2: Where Protestant traditions differ

I found no clear disagreement between denominations in this chapter. The closest things I found:
- **v. 18:** StudyLight lists commentators on this verse by tradition: Calvinist (e.g. Geneva Study Bible), Arminian (e.g. Whedon), Dispensational, Lutheran and Catholic. But the excerpts I saw don't show them actually disagreeing, and the full page wouldn't load. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/6-18.html
- **v. 19:** The moral question about Elisha's deception is discussed by the Anglican Pulpit Commentary and by Guzik (Calvary Chapel). Both accept it, but neither frames it as a denominational difference. (URLs as in v. 19 above.)

## Part 3: Other views

I found nothing from bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org notes, newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org, and nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. Two well-known debates did come up in the evangelical and older commentaries:

- **v. 18, what kind of blindness:**
  - **Confusion, not loss of sight:** The Pulpit Commentary says it was a state of confusion, since the soldiers could follow Elisha 12 miles. Barnes calls it a state of illusion in which a man sees things otherwise than as they are. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/6-18.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/2-kings-6.html
  - **Partial blindness:** Poole (quoted by Guzik) thinks they simply could not make out the man they were looking for. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-6/
  - **Truly blind:** A bible.org series by contrast says God blinded the whole army, leaving it completely helpless. — https://bible.org/seriespage/life-and-times-elisha-prophet%E2%80%94-saved-syrians-war-never-happened-2-kings-61-23
- **v. 25, "dove's dung":**
  - **A plant:** Most older commentators follow Bochart, who thought it was a kind of pulse or chickpea. Benson, Clarke and Gill take this view. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/6-25.htm
  - **Real droppings:** Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary allow or prefer the literal meaning, noting that people have eaten dung in sieges. Constable thinks "dove's dung" is a better translation than the NIV's "seed pods." — https://biblehub.com/2_kings/6-25.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/6-28.html
  - **Fuel or salt:** Gill reports that some Jewish writers thought it was bought for fuel, and Josephus and Theodoret for salt. Gill rejects both. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/6-25.htm
  - **Summary:** GotQuestions gives an overview of the debate and notes the NIV takes the plant reading. — https://www.gotquestions.org/dove-droppings-five-shekels-silver.html

**Gaps:** I have no notes for v. 4 or v. 26 specifically. Gill's commentary appears only in excerpts quoted on other pages.
